title: New practice problems using Tables B.3 and B.4
assumptions: Ideal liquid solution and ideal-gas vapor for mixture calculations.
Raoult’s law: y_i P = x_i P_i^sat.
Convert mmHg to kPa using P_kPa=P_mmHg×101.325/760.
At a bubble point x=z; at a dew point y=z. These are separate boundary states, not the same equilibrium pair.
Every requested state and root lies inside the supplied property-data ranges; extrapolation is disabled.

examples.title: Aromatic mixture: bubble and dew points

questions.prompt: At 75°C, calculate each pure-component saturation pressure. For a liquid with x=(0.50,0.30,0.20), find the bubble pressure and the first vapor composition.
In a separate experiment, start with vapor y=(0.50,0.30,0.20) at 75°C. Find the dew pressure and the first liquid-drop composition.

For overall composition z=(0.50,0.30,0.20), find the bubble and dew temperatures at 40.00 kPa. At the bubble point use x=z; at the dew point use y=z. Report the incipient phase composition at each boundary.
Determine the phase region of a 100.0 mol sample at 75°C and 40.00 kPa. Extension: calculate the amounts and compositions of its liquid and vapor phases.

examples.title: Benzene + toluene: P–x–y and T–x–y diagrams

questions.prompt: At 60°C, construct a P–x–y table at x_B=0,0.20,0.40,0.60,0.80,1.00. For each row calculate P=x_B P_B^sat+(1−x_B)P_T^sat and y_B=x_B P_B^sat/P. Plot P versus x_B and P versus y_B.
At 30.00 kPa, construct a T–x–y table at the same six liquid compositions. Solve the bubble-temperature equation for every row, then calculate y_B. Plot T versus x_B and T versus y_B.
A 100.0 mol mixture with z_B=0.500 is at 60°C and 30.00 kPa. Use a horizontal tie line to find x_B and y_B, then use the lever rule to find liquid and vapor amounts.
For z_B=0.500 at 30.00 kPa, calculate the bubble and dew temperatures and identify where the state in part (c) lies between them.

examples.title: Three hydrocarbons within a shared property-data range

questions.prompt: At 60°C, use x=(0.40,0.35,0.25) to calculate the bubble pressure and first vapor composition of n-hexane/n-heptane/n-octane.
For a separate vapor with y=(0.40,0.35,0.25) at 60°C, calculate the dew pressure and first liquid composition.
For overall composition z=(0.40,0.35,0.25), calculate both boundary temperatures at 34.00 kPa. Verify that both lie in the shared interval 52.9–69.5°C.
Classify a 100.0 mol sample at 60°C and 34.00 kPa. Extension: find its liquid and vapor amounts and compositions.
Assume an ideal liquid solution and ideal vapor. For equimolar methanol/ethanol at 70.00 kPa, calculate the bubble and dew temperatures.
At 62.50°C, calculate the bubble and dew pressures for the equimolar composition and classify a 100.0 mol sample at 70.00 kPa.
At 62.50°C and 70.00 kPa, find the equilibrium liquid/vapor compositions and amounts.
Construct a T–x–y table at 70.00 kPa for x_M=0,0.20,0.40,0.60,0.80,1.00. State the ideal-solution assumption; do not interpret the calculation as measured real-mixture VLE.

examples.title: Liquid-water vapor pressure from Table B.3

questions.prompt: Use the liquid-water portion of Table B.3 to read the saturation pressure at 4.3°C and at 25.0°C. Report each pressure in mmHg and kPa.
Estimate the saturation pressure at 25.35°C by linear interpolation between the 25.3°C and 25.4°C entries. Show the temperature fraction and pressure increment.
Using Table B.3, find the saturation temperature at 101.325 kPa (=760.00 mmHg). Explain why the pure-fluid bubble and dew temperatures coincide.
Classify water at 25°C and 101.325 kPa. At 100°C and the same pressure, can temperature and pressure alone determine how much is liquid and how much is vapor?

answers.explanation: At 25°C, total pressure exceeds the pure-water saturation pressure, so the equilibrium state is liquid. At the saturation state, liquid and vapor have the same composition (pure water); another independent quantity, such as specific volume or total enthalpy, is needed to determine their amounts.
